title: Arithmetic Models for Commodity Futures, Vanilla, and Calendar Spread Options
abstract: We develop an arithmetic multi-factor stochastic volatility model for commodity futures and options. The arithmetic specification yields a low-dimensional Markovian representation of the futures curve and semi-closed-form pricing formulas for vanilla and basket options, including calendar spread options. These properties make the model suitable for large-scale empirical estimation. We estimate the model using an unscented Kalman filter on a panel of WTI crude oil futures, vanilla options, and calendar spread options spanning 2013-2024. We find that three stochastic volatility factors are needed to capture both the level and slope of the volatility term structure, and that hedges based on these factors remove almost all of the daily risk of a portfolio of vanilla options. Calendar spread options provide information about the dependence structure of futures prices that is not captured by futures and vanilla options alone. A model estimated without calendar spread options systematically overprices them by overstating the decorrelation between adjacent futures contracts. Including these options in the estimation brings the model's decorrelation close to the observed decorrelation, which removes the overpricing and improves their hedges, at only a small loss of accuracy in the pricing and hedging of vanilla options. Finally, we show that the arithmetic model fits futures and vanilla options better than its geometric counterpart and hedges the vanilla options slightly better.

title: DerivFlow Finance: option pricing and risk in Python
abstract: A Python library for European and American option pricing, Greeks, implied volatility, Monte Carlo with variance reduction, barrier and Asian options, the Heston model, volatility surfaces and portfolio VaR, with results cross-checked against QuantLib, py_vollib and published reference values.

title: Call Option Price using Pearson Diffusion Processes
abstract: This study introduces a framework for pricing European call options using Pearson diffusion processes with linear drift and quadratic squared diffusion. This class of diffusion processes follows Pearson type IV distribution as its invariant distribution which can effectively capture skewness and excess kurtosis, key empirical features of financial returns. We verify the Novikov condition for risk-neutral measure, and establish the existence of a unique strong solution of stock prices under this measure. We apply the method to Nifty 50 index options and find encouraging results compared to the Black-Scholes and Heston models.

title: Dynamic Scenario-Based Portfolio Optimization for Multi-Asset ETFs
abstract: Portfolio outcomes may depend as much on trading restrictions as on how returns are modeled. We compared historical moving-window returns with conditional scenarios from ARMA--GARCH models and a Student-$t$ copula for 30 U.S.-listed exchange-traded funds. Matched mean--variance and conditional value-at-risk portfolios were evaluated under long-only and limited long--short bounds over 946 sessions. Historical portfolios had higher observed reward--risk ratios in most comparisons, but no paired difference remained significant after multiple-testing adjustment. Conditional scenarios did not consistently reduce realized downside risk. We distinguished changes in target weights from trades required to rebalance holdings after market movements. Relaxing the target-adjustment limit changed exposures, turnover, and some returns more than varying scenario count or seed in the examined tests. These findings suggest that assessments of conditional return inputs should consider portfolio constraints and trading requirements.

title: Remodeling and Application of Stock Option Price Based on Skewed Laplace Distribution Approach
abstract: This paper proposed a new model to price a stock option based on the Skewed Laplace distribution approach (SLOP). The approach was considered to provide a better option price than Black Scholes Option Price (BSOP) because Skewed Laplace distribution (SL) has a shape parameter that can capture excess skewness and kurtosis frequently found in stock return underlying the option price. In this study, SL’s shape parameter was estimated using a mixture of the Moment Method and Fourth-Order Taylor Series approach. The estimator was different from the majority of prior SL’s shape parameter that was obtained by Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). The proposed shape parameter was easier to obtain relative to the prior parameter because it did not require a Likelihood Function (LH) and the maximization of LH where involved a complicated numerical method. The performance of SLOP was applied to eleven different enterprises that trade stock options at several strike prices. According to the empirical results in this research, it can be summarized that the SL approach yields a better option price model rather than Black Scholes (BS).

title: A Comparative Analysis of Three Quantitative Pricing Frameworks for SSE 50ETF Options: BS Analytical Model, CRR Binomial Tree Model and Monte Carlo Simulation
abstract: This study compares the effectiveness and feasibility of the Black-Scholes (BS) analytical model, the Cox-Ross-Rubinstein (CRR) binomial-tree model and Monte Carlo simulation of SSE 50 ETF European call contracts. With the help of the no-arbitrage condition, risk-neutral valuation and geometric Brownian motion are used to create these three models in Python with the same benchmark parameters and later compare their pricing accuracy, convergence rate and algorithmic efficiency, and their applicability to various applications. The numerical data shows that the three methods give almost the same option price: 0.0846 to the BS model, 0.0847 the 200-step CRR model, and 0.0843 the Monte Carlo simulation of 100, 000 paths. The BS approach is by nature simple and easy to use, but has some limitations. As the number of iterations increases, the CRR framework is inclined to the BS value and thus can be used in American style options. High-dimensional and path-dependent derivatives are best modeled using Monte Carlo simulation, whose accuracy depends on the number of simulated paths and the traditional model is not able to price American contracts directly. These results explain the tradeoff between accuracy, flexibility and computational cost in option pricing model selection.

title: Timing the Window: A gated regime engine for issuance and rotation in crypto-asset markets — architecture, calibration from operator heuristics, and conditional derivations for cascade rotation and treasury-levered equity exposure
abstract: Capital markets open and close windows capriciously, and an issuer who must act once, irreversibly, has a different problem from a trader who may act continuously. This paper formalises an instrument built to decide the first problem: an admission clock that states, at any date, whether the window for placing a new instrument is open, how far open, and what dose that grade permits. The instrument is a conjunction of three gates — internal readiness, market regime, and a veto list — and not a weighted index, a design choice we defend on the ground that averaging allows an open gate to compensate a closed one, which is precisely the error an irreversible act cannot absorb. The regime gate is driven by a latent-factor engine whose identification rests on a point we believe has been underweighted in practice: an index assembled exclusively from indicators endogenous to the crypto market measures a single factor that is itself a transformation of the price level, and therefore carries no information about the future willingness of capital to finance an unseasoned instrument. We show that the primary equity issuance market supplies an exogenous and leading measurement of that same latent variable, and that the relevant measurement is the count and receptivity of small deals rather than aggregate proceeds — a distinction the 2026 data make vivid, with record United States proceeds accompanied by a thirty-four per cent fall in the number of deals priced. The paper's technical core converts the tacit knowledge of a daily operator into testable propositions. We obtain three results worth isolating. First, under a margin buffer set proportionally to the prevailing volatility level, the probability that a carry position breaches its buffer is exactly invariant to the level of volatility and depends, to second order, only on the volatility of volatility; the dependence is strictly increasing when the buffer exceeds √2 standard deviations and reverses below it. This gives the lockability gate a defensible threshold variable and explains why a carry bid withdraws in unstable markets without any change in the mean level of risk. Second, the rotation cascade that carries capital from bitcoin outward to the market's tail is asymmetric in its lag structure, not merely in sign: in expansion it propagates head-to-tail with a positive and tier-increasing lag, which is what makes it exploitable and what gives an issuer warning; in contraction it propagates at lag zero with ampli

title: Intraday Forecasting Ability and Liquidity Provision of Institutional Traders
abstract: This study uses a high-frequency dataset from a stock exchange to examine how forecasting ability and liquidity provision relate to institutional traders' proprietary intraday profitability. We discover persistent forecasting abilities among traders. Specifically, we demonstrate that hypothetical flow-following strategies based on the execution flows of these skillful traders yield annualized Sharpe ratios ranging from 16 to 63 across various trading frequencies. We match buy and sell executions into positions, linking realized profit and loss (P&L) to horizon-matched forecasting proxies and the liquidity roles of both executions. Our findings indicate a direct correlation between improved forecasting ability and profitability, where a one-standard-deviation increase in the forecasting ability proxy is associated with 1.02 -- 1.19 currency units higher P&L per matched position. Additionally, we measure liquidity-provision intensity within a matched position by its number of passive executions: zero, one, or two. In these regressions, P&L is 1.28 -- 1.31 currency units higher for one passive execution than for none, and a further 3.79 -- 3.82 higher for two than for one, underscoring the significant financial benefits of liquidity provision.

title: Equilibria and Learning in Competitive Market Making
abstract: We propose a market-making game played among $N \ge 2$ strategic market makers and a single non-strategic representative trader. In a continuous quote space, standard finite-game arguments do not apply, while non-convex and discontinuous payoffs rule out classical continuous existence results and complicate learning. Nonetheless, we characterize pure-strategy Nash equilibria (PSNEs) and show that at least one PSNE always exists under minimal assumptions on the underlying asset value distribution, and that the equilibrium bid-ask spread widens strictly with asset value volatility. To obtain a tractable learning framework, we discretize prices and, under an additional regularity condition, show that the time-averaged play of no-internal-regret learners approaches the continuous Nash price envelope as the tick size vanishes. Finally, we empirically validate our theoretical results through numerical simulations.

title: Feasible sub-replicating portfolios for basket options via the block rearrangement algorithm
abstract: We construct sub-replicating portfolios of vanilla options for a basket call when the marginal distributions of the underlying assets are known and their dependence is not. To do so, we reduce the n-asset problem to n two-asset problems of the type solved by Hobson, Laurence, and Wang (2005a), and use the Block Rearrangement Algorithm1 (BRA) to approximate the minimising dependence among the assets. The cash component of the portfolio is computed exactly, so that its price is a valid lower bound, and reassembling the BRA output with the original marginals gives an upper bound computed by quadrature; together they bracket the minimum basket-option price. In log-normal examples with three and six assets the bracket has a relative width of at most 0.1%, and the corresponding sub-replicating portfolios are sparse, using only two strikes per asset, while the resulting bounds are tighter than those obtained from a general-purpose multi-marginal optimal-transport algorithm with strikes on a grid. We also give the lower bound and an optimal portfolio in closed form in three special cases: a deep in-the-money basket, a basket with one dominant asset, and jointly mixable marginals.

title: Amortized Neural Filtering for Calibrated Posteriors in Statistical Arbitrage
abstract: Statistical arbitrage trades on an estimate of the state of a residual spread, and conventional practice discards the uncertainty of that estimate. We keep the uncertainty and use it in the trading decision. A Neural Filter Estimator (NFE) is trained on simulated paths of a mean-reverting process whose innovation law is selected by testing candidates against real residuals; once trained, it returns the posterior over the latent state of every spread in a cross-section in one forward pass. Three results follow. On simulated paths with known truth, every practical estimator, ours included, falls in one narrow band of accuracy well below an estimator given full information, so the posterior gains no accuracy over a point estimate; its contribution is a correct account of its own uncertainty. On Korean equities, net of costs, the conventional point estimate forecasts about a thousand basis points per holding period more than it realizes, and the amortized methods cut that gap by a factor of roughly two to eight. Sizing positions from the posterior on the same learned factors as the end-to-end Attention Factor Model matches the Sharpe ratio of those factors under the base rule within the period's noise, at no more risk.

title: Feasibility Bounds for Option-Hedged BNPL Lending with Volatile Collateral
abstract: This paper derives and empirically evaluates algebraic feasibility bounds for option-hedged buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) lending secured by volatile collateral. In a merchant-fee-funded lending structure, the bounds identify loan-to-value ratios consistent with option strikes, observed put premiums, loan maturities, and a specified residual-loss budget. The framework encompasses over-protective, exact, and under-protective hedges and is applied to historical Deribit ETH put transactions and ETH spot prices from January 2021 to August 2025. Feasibility increases with merchant fees and is generally stronger at shorter maturities. Although many individual option observations fail the zero-loss screen, the option chain frequently contains at least one feasible quote on an observed date. Allowing bounded residual losses expands feasibility only modestly. An execution-price sensitivity analysis quantifies how increases in protection costs narrow feasible lending intervals and eliminate feasibility for some initially admissible options, with differences across maturities. Because historical closing prices represent last recorded transactions rather than verified executable ask quotations, these results assess historical price-based feasibility, not hedge executability. The framework provides an origination-time screening tool rather than a complete model of commercial lending profitability. JEL classification numbers: G13, G23. Keywords: Collateralized Lending, BNPL, Option hedging, Loan-to-value, Feasibility bounds, Volatile collateral.

title: Implementing BBNJ across fisheries institutions: policy options for interoperable ocean governance
abstract: The entry into force of the Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement) creates a practical implementation problem for fisheries governance. Biodiversity information, area-based management, environmental assessment, fisheries authorization, vessel identity, port measures, maritime safety and market controls are governed by institutions that were not designed as a single compliance system. This Policy and Practice Review uses a structured qualitative institutional appraisal to compare four governance architectures—autonomous implementation, centralized integration, sectoral liaison, and federated interoperability with phased implementation. The method specifies a source hierarchy, four units of comparison, six pre-defined criteria, and an evidence-to-finding protocol that distinguishes existing-authority fit, conditional adaptation and structural constraint. Each finding is tied to treaty text, official institutional material and relevant peer-reviewed scholarship available through 31 August 2026. The legal foundation for cross-regime coexistence is anchored in BBNJ Agreement articles 5(2), 22, 29, 47(6)(c) and 51, which combine non-undermining, cooperation and coordination, respect for institutional competences, and links to existing information mechanisms. The comparison does not claim to predict governmental policy choices or empirically prove an optimal design. Instead, it identifies institutionally workable options under stated legal and administrative constraints. On that basis, federated interoperability is carried forward as a conditional policy proposition for staged testing, subject to provenance controls, verification and legal assessment by the competent authorities, cybersecurity, capacity support and review. The article proposes a three-stage pathway—pre-COP mapping, first-COP institutionalization, and post-COP pilots and review—linking BBNJ bodies, RFMOs, FAO/PSMA mechanisms, IMO-related systems and national administrations.

title: Active Risk Management
abstract: This chapter examines the role of active risk management in institutional portfolios. It begins by distinguishing passive exposure to the market returns, or beta, from active decisions intended to generate alpha. The chapter then develops the idea of alpha–beta separation and shows how active returns can arise from asset allocation, security selection, and their interaction. Building on this foundation, it introduces return attribution methods, including the Brinson framework, and explains how tracking error measures the volatility of performance relative to a benchmark rather than total portfolio risk. The chapter also discusses how benchmark design, especially the distinction between fixed-weight and floating-weight benchmarks, shapes manager incentives, performance evaluation, and governance. Particular attention is given to the different nature of active risk in public and private markets, where liquidity, valuation frequency, and implementation flexibility differ materially. The chapter concludes by considering how institutional investors can allocate and budget active risk across the total portfolio, distinguishing structural active risk from manager active risk and linking active risk taking to governance, capacity, and expected information ratios.

title: Comparative viral inactivation kinetics of electron beam and gamma irradiation and functional characterization of electron beam inactivated viruses
abstract: Introduction Electron beam (eBeam) technology is increasingly being adopted in biomedical research and industry as an alternative to cobalt-60-based gamma irradiation. However, a comprehensive understanding of how eBeam energy and dose influence viral inactivation and the preservation of viral surface antigens remains limited. This study compared the inactivation kinetics of human rotavirus (RV), human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and influenza A virus (IAV) following exposure to high-energy electron beam (HEEB; 10 MeV), medium-energy electron beam (MEEB; 4.5 MeV), and gamma irradiation under conditions that were standardized to the greatest extent possible. Additionally, antigenic characterization was performed for HEEB and MEEB inactivated viruses. Methods Human rotavirus, human respiratory syncytial virus, and influenza A virus were irradiated using HEEB, MEEB and gamma irradiation using incremental doses under standardized experimental conditions. Viral inactivation kinetics (D 10 ) were determined using TCID 50 assays while preservation of viral antigenicity and virus–host receptor interactions were evaluated by hemagglutination and ELISA assays. Heat and formalin inactivation were used as experimental controls. Results All three modalities effectively inactivated the tested viruses with comparable overall inactivation efficiency. The D 10 values of RV (1.23–1.29 kGy) and RSV (1.03–1.73 kGy) did not differ significantly ( p = 0.01) among the irradiation modalities. The IAV exhibited greater radioresistance, with D 10 value ranging between 1.62–2.27 kGy. Complete inactivation by both high- and medium-energy eBeam was confirmed by three serial passages. Importantly, eBeam-treated viruses retained viral antigenicity (VP4, F-protein, and HA) at levels comparable to untreated controls, whereas heat and formalin treatments reduced antigenicity by 5.09- to 256-fold and 1.26- to 2-fold, respectively. Furthermore, eBeam-inactivated viruses exhibited 1.54- to 23.11-fold greater virus-host receptor recognition than heat and formalin inactivated preparations. Discussion Both high-energy and medium-energy electron beam modalities achieved viral inactivation efficiencies comparable to gamma irradiation under standardized conditions, supporting their potential as non-radioisotopic alternatives for viral inactivation. Importantly, eBeam treatment preserved viral antigenicity and functional virus–host receptor interactions more effectively than conventional heat

title: Marginal Specification and Tail Dependence in Equity Markets
abstract: Copula conclusions for equity markets depend on both marginal filtering and the temporal pairing of daily returns. We analyse S&P 500, FTSE 100, and Nikkei 225 returns from 2010 to 2025 in three pairwise panels. A rolling 756-day training and 63-day evaluation design compares empirical-CDF, Gaussian-GARCH, and Student-t-GARCH margins. The GARCH filters use a standard one-step-ahead recursion, and every candidate copula is estimated by pseudo maximum likelihood. The Student-t copula has the highest window-weighted density score under all three margins, with scores of 0.0924, 0.0703, and 0.0685. It is the numerical winner in eight of nine panel–margin cells, but paired moving-block intervals support a positive advantage in only three cells. A lead–lag check materially changes the S&P 500–Nikkei 225 association, while a joint-downside probability score does not select the same family as the density score. The evidence therefore supports specification-aware conditional-dependence analysis, rather than an invariant model ranking or causal contagion claim.

title: Model Risk in European Union Allowance Futures and Options: From Black–76 to Institutionally Grounded Models—A Critical Structured Review
abstract: Pricing models for European Union Allowance (EUA) derivatives are often assessed as statistical specifications even though the EU Emissions Trading System changes the payoff boundary, supply process, and intertemporal value of the underlying compliance asset. This critical structured review examines how EUA futures and options models have developed from Black–76 conventions to institutionally grounded equilibrium, structural, and Market Stability Reserve (MSR) specifications; how regulatory mechanisms enter risk-neutral valuation; and what evidence supports model robustness. Fifty-three DOI- or publisher-verified academic records were coded using an Institution–Model–Measure–Evidence (IMME) lens: 47 inform the model-level synthesis and six provide contextual triangulation. The evidence is organized into early benchmarks and deficiencies, institutionally grounded models, and MSR-era pricing and validation. Black–76 remains a transparent quotation benchmark, but evidence from physical-measure dynamics and phase boundaries limits its structural interpretation. Structural and equilibrium models make institutional channels explicit, yet add identification and numerical risks. Comparative studies provide some held-out pricing evidence, but the literature still lacks transaction-cost-aware hedging and regime-transport tests. The resulting model-selection principle is conditional adequacy: use the least complex model that is regime-aligned, measure-explicit, empirically identified, and validated for the intended pricing or hedging task.

title: Financial Time-Series Forecasting: Towards Synergizing Performance And Interpretability Within a Hybrid Machine Learning Approach
abstract: Abstract In the realm of cryptocurrency, the prediction of Bitcoin prices has garnered substantial attention due to its potential impact on financial markets and investment strategies. This paper propose a comparative study on hybrid machine learning algorithms and leverage on enhancing model interpretability. Specifically, linear regression(OLS, LASSO), long-short term memory(LSTM), decision tree regressors are introduced. Through the grounded experiments, we observe linear regressor achieves the best performance among candidate models. For the interpretability, we carry out a systematic overview on the preprocessing techniques of time-series statistics, including decomposition, auto-correlational function, exponential triple forecasting, which aim to excavate latent relations and complex patterns appeared in the financial time-series forecasting. We believe this work may derive more attention and inspire more researches in the realm of time-series analysis and its realistic applications.

title: Essays in financial economics
abstract: In the first paper of my dissertation I study the size and source of exchange-traded funds’ (ETFs) price impact in the most ETF-dominated asset classes: volatility (VIX) and commodities. I show that the introduction of ETFs increased futures prices. To identify ETF-induced price distortions, I propose a model-independent approach to replicate the value of a VIX futures contract. This allows me to isolate a nonfundamental component in VIX futures prices, of 18.5% per year, that is strongly related to the rebalancing of ETFs. To understand the source of that component, I decompose trading demand from ETFs into three main parts: leverage rebalancing, calendar rebalancing, and flow rebalancing. Leverage rebalancing has the largest effects. It amplifies price changes and introduces unhedgeable risks for ETF counterparties. Surprisingly, providing liquidity to leveraged ETFs turns out to be a bet on variance, even in a market with a zero net share of ETFs. Trading against leverage rebalancing delivers large abnormal returns and Sharpe ratios above two across markets. The second paper analyses the impact of the ECB’s Corporate Sector Purchase Programme (CSPP) announcement on prices, liquidity and debt issuance in the European corporate bond market. I find that the quantitative easing (QE) programme increased prices and liquidity of bonds eligible to be purchased substantially. Bond yields dropped on average by 30 bps (8%) after the CSPP announcement. Tri-party repo turnover rose by 8.15 million USD (29%), and bilateral turnover went up by 7.05 million USD (72%). Bid-ask spreads also showed significant liquidity improvement in eligible bonds. QE was successful in boosting corporate debt issuance. Firms issued 2.19 billion EUR (25%) more in QE-eligible debt after the CSPP announcement, compared to other types of debt. Surprisingly, corporates used the attracted funds mostly to increase dividends. These effects were more pronounced for longer-maturity, lower-rated bonds, and for more credit-constrained, lower-rated firms. The third paper (co-authored with Christian Julliard, Zijun Liu, Seyed E. Seyedan and Kathy Yuan) studies the determinants of repo haircuts in the UK market. We find that transaction maturity and collateral quality have first order importance. We also document that counterparties matter in determining haircuts. Hedge funds, as borrowers, receive significantly higher haircuts. Larger borrowers with higher ratings receive lower haircuts, but we find

title: Stock Market Prediction Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques: A Review
abstract: The rapid advancement of machine learning and deep learning techniques has revolutionized stock market prediction, providing innovative methods to analyze financial trends and market behavior. This review paper presents a comprehensive analysis of various machine learning and deep learning approaches utilized in stock market prediction, focusing on their methodologies, evaluation metrics, and datasets. Popular models such as LSTM, CNN, and SVM are examined, highlighting their strengths and limitations in predicting stock prices, volatility, and trends. Additionally, we address persistent challenges, including data quality and model interpretability, and explore emerging research directions to overcome these obstacles. This study aims to summarize the current state of research, provide insights into the effectiveness of predictive models.

title: COVID-19 pandemic and the crude oil market risk: hedging options with non-energy financial innovations
abstract: This study examines the hedging effectiveness of financial innovations against crude oil investment risks, both before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. We focus on the non-energy exchange traded funds (ETFs) as proxies for financial innovations given the potential positive correlation between energy variants and crude oil proxies. We employ a multivariate volatility modeling framework that accounts for important statistical features of the non-energy ETFs and oil price series in the computation of optimal weights and optimal hedging ratios. Results show evidence of hedging effectiveness for the financial innovations against oil market risks, with higher hedging performance observed during the pandemic. Overall, we show that sectoral financial innovations provide resilient investment options. Therefore, we propose that including the ETFs in an investment portfolio containing oil could improve risk-adjusted returns, especially in similar financial crisis as witnessed during the pandemic. In essence, our results are useful for investors in the global oil market seeking to maximize risk-adjusted returns when making investment decisions. Moreover, by exploring the role of structural breaks in the multivariate volatility framework, our attempts at establishing robustness for the results reveal that ignoring the same may lead to wrong conclusions about the hedging effectiveness.

title: Machine Learning-Powered Smart Healthcare Systems in the Era of Big Data: Applications, Diagnostic Insights, Challenges, and Ethical Implications
abstract: Healthcare data rapidly increases, and patients seek customized, effective healthcare services. Big data and machine learning (ML) enabled smart healthcare systems hold revolutionary potential. Unlike previous reviews that separately address AI or big data, this work synthesizes their convergence through real-world case studies, cross-domain ML applications, and a critical discussion on ethical integration in smart diagnostics. The review focuses on the role of big data analysis and ML towards better diagnosis, improved efficiency of operations, and individualized care for patients. It explores the principal challenges of data heterogeneity, privacy, computational complexity, and advanced methods such as federated learning (FL) and edge computing. Applications in real-world settings, such as disease prediction, medical imaging, drug discovery, and remote monitoring, illustrate how ML methods, such as deep learning (DL) and natural language processing (NLP), enhance clinical decision-making. A comparison of ML models highlights their value in dealing with large and heterogeneous healthcare datasets. In addition, the use of nascent technologies such as wearables and Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) is examined for their role in supporting real-time data-driven delivery of healthcare. The paper emphasizes the pragmatic application of intelligent systems by highlighting case studies that reflect up to 95% diagnostic accuracy and cost savings. The review ends with future directions that seek to develop scalable, ethical, and interpretable AI-powered healthcare systems. It bridges the gap between ML algorithms and smart diagnostics, offering critical perspectives for clinicians, data scientists, and policymakers.

title: Supervised machine learning for theory building and testing: Opportunities in operations management
abstract: Abstract Machine learning's (ML's) unique power to approximate functions and identify non‐obvious regularities in data have attracted considerable attention from researchers in natural and social sciences. The emergence of predictive modeling applications in OM studies notwithstanding, it remains unclear how OM scholars can effectively leverage supervised ML for theory building and theory testing, the primary goals of scientific research. We attempt to fill this gap by conducting a literature review of recent developments in supervised ML in OM to identify vacancies in the extant literature, shedding light on how ML applications can move beyond problem‐solving into theory building, and formulating a procedure to help OM scholars leverage ML for exploratory theory development. Our procedure employs the random forest with well‐developed properties and inference toolkits that are crucial for empirical research. We then expand the boundary of ML usage and connect supervised ML to the explanatory modeling and hypothesis testing employed by OM empiricists for decades, and discuss the use of supervised ML for causal inference from observational data. We posit that contemporary ML can facilitate pattern exploration and enhance the validity of theory testing. We conclude by discussing directions for future empirical OM studies that aim to leverage ML.

title: Comparison of ARIMA and Artificial Neural Networks Models for Stock Price Prediction
abstract: This paper examines the forecasting performance of ARIMA and artificial neural networks model with published stock data obtained from New York Stock Exchange. The empirical results obtained reveal the superiority of neural networks model over ARIMA model. The findings further resolve and clarify contradictory opinions reported in literature over the superiority of neural networks and ARIMA model and vice versa.

title: COVID-19 Pandemic and Romanian Stock Market Volatility: A GARCH Approach
abstract: This paper investigates the volatility of daily returns on the Romanian stock market between January 2020 and April 2021. Volatility is analyzed by means of the representative index for Bucharest Stock Exchange (BSE), namely, the Bucharest Exchange Trading (BET) index, along with twelve companies traded on BSE. The quantitative investigation was performed using GARCH approach. In the survey, the GARCH model (1,1) was applied to explore the volatility of the BET and BSE traded shares. Conditional volatility for the daily return series showed noticeable evidence of volatility that shifts over the explored period. In the first quarter of 2020, the Romanian equity market volatility increased to a level very close to that recorded during the global financial crisis of 2007–2009. Over the next two quarters, volatility had a downward trend. Besides, after VAR estimation, no causal connection was found among the COVID-19 variables and the BET index.

title: Designing multi-sensory displays for abstract data
abstract: The rapid increase in available information has lead to many attempts to automatically locate patterns in large, abstract, multi-attributed information spaces. These techniques are often called data mining and have met with varying degrees of success. An alternative approach to automatic pattern detection is to keep the user in the exploration loop by developing displays for perceptual data mining. This approach allows a domain expert to search the data for useful relationships and can be effective when automated rules are hard to define. However, designing models of the abstract data and defining appropriate displays are critical tasks in building a useful system. Designing displays of abstract data is especially difficult when multi-sensory interaction is considered. New technology, such as Virtual Environments, enables such multi-sensory interaction. For example, interfaces can be designed that immerse the user in a 3D space and provide visual, auditory and haptic (tactile) feedback. It has been a goal of Virtual Environments to use multi-sensory interaction in an attempt to increase the human-to-computer bandwidth. This approach may assist the user to understand large information spaces and find patterns in them. However, while the motivation is simple enough, actually designing appropriate mappings between the abstract information and the human sensory channels is quite difficult. Designing intuitive multi-sensory displays of abstract data is complex and needs to carefully consider human perceptual capabilities, yet we interact with the real world everyday in a multi-sensory way. Metaphors can describe mappings between the natural world and an abstract information space. This thesis develops a division of the multi-sensory design space called the MS-Taxonomy. The MS-Taxonomy provides a concept map of the design space based on temporal, spatial and direct metaphors. The detailed concepts within the taxonomy allow for discussion of low level design issues. Furthermore the concepts abstract to higher levels, allowing general design issues to be compared and discussed across the different senses. The MS-Taxonomy provides a categorisation of multi-sensory design options. However, to design effective multi-sensory displays requires more than a thorough understanding of design options. It is also useful to have guidelines to follow, and a process to describe the design steps. This thesis uses the structure of the MS-Taxonomy to develop the MS-Guidelines and

title: Applying Machine Learning in Retail Demand Prediction—A Comparison of Tree-Based Ensembles and Long Short-Term Memory-Based Deep Learning
abstract: In the realm of retail supply chain management, accurate forecasting is paramount for informed decision making, as it directly impacts business operations and profitability. This study delves into the application of tree-based ensemble forecasting, specifically using extra tree Regressors (ETRs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. Utilizing over six years of historical demand data from a prominent retail entity, the dataset encompasses daily demand metrics for more than 330 products, totaling 5.2 million records. Additionally, external variables, such as meteorological and COVID-19-related data, are integrated into the analysis. Our evaluation, spanning three perishable product categories, reveals that the ETR model outperforms LSTM in metrics including MAPE, MAE, RMSE, and R2. This disparity in performance is particularly pronounced for fresh meat products, whereas it is marginal for fruit products. These ETR results were evaluated alongside three other tree-based ensemble methods, namely XGBoost, Random Forest Regression (RFR), and Gradient Boosting Regression (GBR). The comparable performance across these four tree-based ensemble techniques serves to reinforce their comparative analysis with LSTM-based deep learning models. Our findings pave the way for future studies to assess the comparative efficacy of tree-based ensembles and deep learning techniques across varying forecasting horizons, such as short-, medium-, and long-term predictions.

title: Design Principles for Policy Mixes: Cohesion and Coherence in ‘New Governance Arrangements’
abstract: Abstract New Governance Arrangements (NGAs) have emerged as a lively topic in comparative policy studies and are often proposed as solutions to complex policy problems like environmental or health protection. However, assessing the merits and demerits of particular arrangements or instrument mixes is difficult. The paper proposes a variety of tools to tackle the often-overlooked problem of identifying and inventorying the instruments found in instrument mixes and assessing their likelihood to produce optimal results. A framework is developed for evaluating the likelihood of successful implementation of NGA's that exploits the fact that new policy development is almost always constrained by previous policy choices which have become institutionalized. The degree to which this institutionalization has occurred is seen as variable and the implementation to depend on a number of well-understood processes such as increasing returns and other kinds of positive feedback; sunk costs; and incremental policy learning. The applicability of the framework is demonstrated in the context of NGAs found in the forestry sector.

title: Recurrent Neural Networks: A Comprehensive Review of Architectures, Variants, and Applications
abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have significantly advanced the field of machine learning by enabling the effective processing of sequential data. This paper provides a comprehensive review of RNNs and their applications, highlighting advancements in architectures such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM), and stacked LSTM. The study examines the application of RNNs in different domains, including natural language processing (NLP), speech recognition, financial time series forecasting, bioinformatics, autonomous vehicles, and anomaly detection. Additionally, the study discusses recent innovations, such as the integration of attention mechanisms and the development of hybrid models that combine RNNs with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformer architectures. This review aims to provide machine learning researchers and practitioners with a comprehensive overview of the current state and future directions of RNN research.

title: Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs)
abstract: Over nearly a quarter of a century, ETFs have become one of the most popular passive investment vehicles among retail and professional investors due to their low transaction costs and high liquidity.By the end of 2016, the market share of ETFs topped over 10% of the total market capitalization traded on US exchanges, while representing more than 30% of the overall trading volume.ETFs revolutionized the asset management industry by taking market share from traditional investment vehicles such as mutual funds and index futures.Because ETFs rely on arbitrage activity to synchronize their prices with the prices of the underlying portfolio, trading activity at the ETF level translates to trading of the underlying securities.Researchers found that while ETFs enhance price discovery, they also inject non-fundamental volatility to market prices and affect the correlation structure of returns.Furthermore, ETFs impact the liquidity of the underlying portfolios, especially during events of market stress.

title: All in the family Nesting symmetric and asymmetric GARCH models
abstract: This paper develops a parametric family of models of generalized autoregressive heteroskedasticity (GARCH). The family nests the most popular symmetric and asymmetric GARCH models, thereby highlighting the relation between the models and their treatment of asymmetry. Furthermore, the structure permits nested tests of different types of asymmetry and functional forms. Daily U.S. stock return data reject all standard GARCH models in favor of a model in which, roughly speaking, the conditional standard deviation depends on the shifted absolute value of the shocks raised to the power three halves and past standard deviations.

title: Put-Call Parity Violations and Market Frictions in China's SSE 50 ETF Options Market: Evidence from the AI Boom of 2023
abstract: This paper empirically investigates the deviation of the put - call parity (PCP) in China's SSE 50ETF options market (510050 XSHG) for the whole year of 2023-when the release of ChatGPT triggered an unprecedented investor sentiment hype of artificial intelligence. Based on 15,604 pairs of matched call-put options covering all 242 trading days, we detected that there was always a systematic and persistent overpricing of calls over put options. We interpret this phenomenon as follows: The explosive market demand by retail investors on call options-a leveraged sentiment on AI-related market bullishness-out-weighted the arbitrage capacity of constrained arbitrageurs by market frictions to make corrections to the mispricing through a reverse arbitrage strategy (selling call options, buying put options, and buying spot options). Using quarterly dummy variables as proxies for AI market sentiment cycle, we found that by controlling time stage variables, the R² rose from 8.9% to 71.67% to confirm that demand dynamics driven by market sentiment rather than the specific features of contracts-are the primary drivers for the variability in the PCP violation phenomena. Compared with the baseline of AI craze hype in the first quarter, the quarterly effect shows monotonically decreasing, while the implied residuals bias the fourth quarter, which is still a positive one. Confirmed is that the permanent structural friction lower limit will persist even after the sentiment premium of AI fades. Our research result provides fresh evidence in terms of behavioral demand shocks' interaction with the institutional friction on in emerging markets, thereby creating option price biases.

title: Multiple Stopping and Exercise Boundaries for American Put Options
abstract: This article studies a finite-horizon American put option with up to $m$ exercise rights under the risk-neutral Black--Scholes model, where consecutive exercises must be separated by a prescribed refractory period $δ>0$ and unused rights may expire. For each number of remaining rights, we show that optimal exercise is characterized by a single exercise boundary and that these boundaries are ordered by the number of remaining rights. We prove optimality of the first boundary-hitting time and establish local Lipschitz continuity of the exercise boundaries within each open deadline strip. Away from the deadlines, we derive smooth fit, the associated quasi-variational inequality and free-boundary formulation, an early-exercise-premium representation, recursive Volterra-type boundary equations, and a verification theorem. We also extend the recursive formulation to an independent random termination time, thereby allowing for exogenous termination of the option contract.
